study_identification_part.si3_author_journal_year: Itälinna et al., PLoS Computational Biology, 2023
study_identification_part.si4_title: Using normative modeling and machine learning for detecting mild traumatic brain injury from magnetoencephalography data

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To investigate the feasibility of using a multivariate machine-learning approach combined with normative modeling of MEG data to detect mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) and to identify patients who would benefit from treatment and rehabilitation.

rci1_dataset_name.supporting_text: A large open neuroimaging dataset by the Cambridge Centre for Ageing and Neuroscience (Cam-CAN) [29], containing MEG and MRI measurements of nearly 700 healthy participants aged 18 to 87, was used for creating the normative reference data.

rci2_hc_n.supporting_text: Subjects with missing or incomplete resting-state MEG measurements or T1-weighted MRI images were excluded from the analyses, resulting in a set of 621 subjects.

rci7_preprocessing_pipeline.supporting_text: The temporal extension of the signal space separation (tSSS) [33] method implemented in the MaxFilter software package (MEGIN Oy) was used for reducing external artifacts in the MEG data... The FastICA algorithm available in MNE-Python software [35] was used for the ICA processing... rci9_quality_checking_detail.reason: The paper provides details on the quality checking methods.
rci9_quality_checking_detail.supporting_text: The temporal extension of the signal space separation (tSSS) [33] method implemented in the MaxFilter software package (MEGIN Oy) was used for reducing external artifacts in the MEG data. To suppress artifacts caused by cardiac activity and eye movement, independent component analysis (ICA) [34] was used for identifying components most prominently related to the aforementioned sources. In most cases, 1-2 components were removed, but for some subjects three or even four components were removed based on manual inspection of the spatial patterns and time courses of the components.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: A support vector machine (SVM) classifier was trained to discriminate between mTBI patients and healthy controls based on the deviation scores. The performance of the classifier was evaluated using nested cross-validation. Permutation feature importance was used to identify the most significant features for the classification. A Mann Whitney U-test was used to assess the relationship between classification results and the presence of MRI lesions.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: The study demonstrates that a combination of normative modeling of MEG data and machine learning can distinguish mTBI patients from healthy controls with an accuracy of 79%, with theta-band activity being the most significant predictor.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: The classifier achieved a mean accuracy of 0.790, with a sensitivity of 0.912 and a specificity of 0.638. The most important features for the classification were found in the theta (4-8 Hz) frequency band, primarily in the parietal, temporal, and occipital lobes. The use of a large normative dataset outperformed age-matched smaller datasets. The approach was able to identify individual-level abnormalities in theta-band activity.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The proposed method could be used to aid in the diagnosis of mTBI, particularly in cases with non-specific and prolonged symptoms. It could also help in identifying patients who might benefit from neuropsychological interventions. The framework is generalizable to other neurological disorders and could be integrated into a clinical decision support system.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: The clinical dataset was small, leading to high variance in the performance metrics. The analysis pipeline was not fully automated due to the manual inspection of ICA components. The interpretability of the non-linear SVM model is limited. The normative and clinical data were collected at different sites, which may have introduced a bias.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: The study provides a good example of applying normative modeling to MEG data for clinical classification. The authors have made their code available, which is a plus for reproducibility. The comparison of different normative data selection strategies (full vs. age-matched) provides valuable insights for future studies.
